s: A company hosts a game player-matching service on a public-facing, physical, on-premises instance that all users are able to access over the instance uses UDP. The company wants to migrate the service to AWS and provide a high level of security. A solutions architect needs to de matching service using AWS. Which combination of steps should the solutions architect take to meet these requirements? (Select THREE.)
o: Use a Network Load Balancer (NLB) in front of the player-matching instance. Use a friendly DNS entry in Amazon Route 53-point address.
Use an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in front of the player-matching instance. Use a friendly DNS entry in Amazon Route 53 p facing fully qualified domain name (FQDN).
Define an AWS WAF rule to explicitly drop non-UDP traffic, and associate the rule with the load balancer.
Configure a network ACL rule to block all non-UDP traffic. Associate the network ACL with the subnets that hold the load balance
e: To migrate a UDP-based public service to AWS with high security: l EC2 instances in private subnets: Deploy the matching service on EC2 instances within private subnets to isolate them from direct internet exposure, improving security posture l Network Load Balancer (NLB) for UDP: NLB is the only AWS load balancer that supports UDP protocol. Application Load Balancer only supports TCP-based protocols (HTTP/HTTPS). Configure NLB with UDP listener on port matching the service l Security Group with UDP rules: Create a security group allowing UDP traffic on the service port from the NLB l NAT Gateway for outbound traffic: If the service needs outbound internet connectivity, configure a NAT Gateway in a public subnet to allow private EC2 instances to initiate outbound connections l Optional: VPC Endpoint or PrivateLink: For additional security, could expose via VPC endpoint rather than public NLB This combination provides UDP protocol support through NLB while maintaining security through private subnets and security groups.
nt: The PDF text of this question is garbled and cut off. It asks for three answers but shows four options and a two-letter key. The intended answer is an NLB (UDP) plus network ACLs that block non-UDP traffic, and usually also Shield or WAF protection.

w.y: The service uses UDP, so only a Network Load Balancer can front it with a friendly Route 53 name. Since AWS WAF does not work with NLBs, a network ACL is the way to drop non-UDP traffic at the subnet.

o.A: Correct: NLB supports UDP and Route 53 gives a friendly DNS name.
o.B: ALB only supports HTTP and HTTPS, not UDP.
o.C: AWS WAF cannot be attached to an NLB and does not inspect UDP.
o.D: Correct: a network ACL that allows only the needed UDP traffic blocks everything else.
